notes.meaning: Solomon married many women from surrounding pagan nations, going far beyond his earlier marriage to Pharaoh's daughter. God had specifically commanded kings not to multiply wives for themselves, but Solomon ignored this limit. By taking wives from nations like Moab, Ammon, and Edom, he opened the door to spiritual danger.

The Lord had strictly warned Israel that marrying people from these nations would lead God's people to worship false gods. In spite of this clear warning, Solomon grew deeply attached to these foreign women. His strong emotional desires overrode the wisdom and obedience he once had.

Solomon gathered seven hundred royal wives and three hundred secondary wives, called concubines. A harem of this size was seen in the ancient world as a grand display of royal power and wealth. Just as God had warned, these many wives slowly pulled his affections away from the Lord.

As Solomon grew older, his wives persuaded him to worship other gods alongside the Lord. Unlike his father David, whose devotion to God remained steady despite personal failures, Solomon's heart was divided. A lifetime of spiritual privileges did not protect him once he allowed his desires to guide him instead of God's word.

Solomon took part in worshipping Ashtoreth, a goddess of the Sidonians linked with immoral rituals, and Milcom, the terrible false god of Ammon. In doing so, Solomon committed evil in the Lord's sight. He failed to follow God completely, falling far short of the wholehearted loyalty his father David had shown.

Solomon built open-air worship centers, called high places, on the Mount of Olives right across from Jerusalem and the temple he had built for God. He set these up for Chemosh, the god of Moab, and Molech, the Ammonite god whose worship involved the sacrifice of children. Sin led the world's wisest king to support the darkest forms of idol worship.

Solomon provided worship sites for each of his foreign wives so they could burn incense and offer sacrifices to their own gods. Once he gave in to pleasing one wife, he felt compelled to do the same for all of them. Catering to false worship to keep peace at home led to an open insult against the true God.

The Lord became angry with Solomon because his heart had deserted the God of Israel. God had personally appeared to Solomon twice to confirm His promises and had explicitly forbidden him from following other gods. Solomon had received greater spiritual privileges than almost anyone else, making his disobedience completely without excuse.

The Lord announced His judgment against Solomon, likely speaking through a prophet. Because Solomon broke God's covenant and ignored His laws, God declared He would tear the kingdom away and hand it over to one of Solomon's own servants. God holds leaders responsible when they abandon His commands.

differ.view: Many in this tradition hold that Solomon later repented and wrote Ecclesiastes as his confession, believing God keeps His chosen ones from falling away finally.
Some in this tradition conclude that Scripture records no repentance for Solomon, indicating he died having fallen away from God.

notes.meaning: God showed mercy by delaying this judgment until after Solomon's death, doing so for the sake of David. The kingdom would instead be torn from the hands of Solomon's son. God remained faithful to His covenant with David, even while punishing the sins of David's royal line.

God promised not to strip away the entire kingdom from Solomon's son, reserving one tribe for David's royal line. This preserved tribe was Judah, which also included the smaller tribe of Benjamin and the city of Jerusalem. God preserved this line so that His promise of an enduring throne for David's descendant would never fail.

The Lord stirred up an adversary against Solomon named Hadad, a member of the royal family of Edom. As long as Solomon remained faithful, God gave his kingdom unbroken peace, but now God allowed enemies to rise. God used human opponents as a rod of discipline to awaken Solomon to his sin.

Years earlier, King David had conquered Edom, and his army commander Joab remained there for six months. Joab carried out a ruthless campaign to kill every male Edomite he could find while burying the fallen soldiers. This severe slaughter created a deep and lasting hatred toward Israel among surviving Edomites.

During Joab's slaughter, some servants of the Edomite king rescued Hadad, who was then only a young boy. They fled southward across the border toward Egypt to escape the sword. God permitted this young prince to escape so that he would later serve as a tool of discipline for Solomon.

Hadad and his escorts traveled through Midian and the desert of Paran, gathering more men along the way. When they arrived in Egypt, Pharaoh welcomed the young prince, giving him land, a house, and food supplies. Pharaoh protected Hadad as an exiled royal who might one day be a useful ally against Israel.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest this passage weaves together two separate stories about an Edomite rebel, or that the name for Egypt in this account might refer to a region in northern Arabia.

notes.meaning: Hadad won such strong favor with Pharaoh that the king gave him his own sister-in-law in marriage. She gave birth to a son named Genubath, whom Queen Tahpenes raised in the royal palace alongside Pharaoh's own sons. Hadad was treated as part of Egypt's royal family, gaining influence and honor in exile.

When Hadad learned that both King David and his fierce commander Joab had died, he asked Pharaoh for permission to return home. Pharaoh was surprised and asked what Hadad lacked in Egypt, but Hadad insisted that he must go back to Edom. Even the comforts and riches of a foreign palace could not erase his longing to reclaim his homeland.
